hypothesis: If the claim holds, every neighbour-independent substitution system in a complete enumerated family (2 colours with replacement blocks of length 1-3; 3 colours with blocks of length 1-2) produces, from a single cell, a sequence whose subword complexity stays bounded (repetitive) or grows at most polynomially slowly (nested), far below the near-exponential subword complexity of rule 30's rows and centre column, so none of them can reproduce rule 30; while a neighbour-dependent substitution system (one output cell per cell, chosen from the cell and its two neighbours) reproduces rules 90 and 30 exactly.
pass_criterion: Pre-registered. For each of the 196 two-colour rules {0 -> w0, 1 -> w1} with |w0|, |w1| in {1,2,3} and each of the 1728 three-colour rules with block lengths in {1,2}, start from a single cell of colour 1 and iterate until the word has >= L = 131072 symbols (or 60 steps if it never does), truncate to L, and compute the number p(n) of distinct length-n factors for n = 1..14. For rule 30 from a single black cell compute p(14) of (i) the central 40001 cells of the row at step 20000 and (ii) the first 65536 cells of the centre column. Build the neighbour-dependent substitution system whose rule maps each cell to one new cell given by the elementary-CA table of its (left, self, right) neighbourhood, and run it for 1000 steps from a single black cell. PASS (supports) if (a) every neighbour-independent rule has p(14) <= 225 = (14+1)^2 (eventually periodic words are those with p(14) = p(13); the rest are counted as nested), (b) both rule 30 sequences have p(14) >= 2000, and (c) the neighbour-dependent systems for rules 90 and 30 reproduce the cellular-automaton rows exactly at every one of the 1000 steps.
fail_criterion: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if any neighbour-independent rule in the family has p(14) >= 2000 (rule-30-like complexity), or if the neighbour-dependent construction does not reproduce rule 90 or rule 30. If some neighbour-independent rule has 225 < p(14) < 2000 the result is 'mixed' and the rule is reported with its complexity profile.
interpretation: 'Repetitive' is operationalised as eventually periodic (bounded subword complexity, Morse-Hedlund), 'nested' as a self-similar word, which for fixed points of morphisms has subword complexity O(n^2) at most (Pansiot); the threshold (n+1)^2 at n = 14 is therefore a generous upper bound for repetitive-or-nested and about a tenth of what a random-like binary sequence of this length shows. 'Cannot emulate rule 30' is tested within the enumerated family by the complexity gap (a word with p(14) <= 225 cannot contain the rule 30 row, whose own p(14) is measured); it is not a proof over all encodings. The neighbour-dependent half is tested exactly as the book describes it (rules 'always yielding just one cell and corresponding quite directly to cellular automata', p. 666).

datasets.name: Enumerated neighbour-independent substitution systems (2 colours, blocks 1-3; 3 colours, blocks 1-2), rule 30 evolutions, and neighbour-dependent substitution emulations of rules 90 and 30, generated by analysis.py

generator.neighbour_independent_family: all maps colour -> block over blocks of length 1..3 on {0,1} (14^2 = 196 rules) and blocks of length 1..2 on {0,1,2} (12^3 = 1728 rules); initial word: single cell of colour 1; words truncated to 131072 symbols
generator.rule30: elementary CA rule 30 (Wolfram numbering) from a single black cell: row at step 20000 (central 40001 cells) and centre column for 65536 steps
generator.neighbour_dependent: each cell replaced by one cell = ECA table(left, self, right), rules 90 and 30, 1000 steps from a single black cell, compared with direct CA evolution
generator.complexity: number of distinct factors of length n = 1..14

datasets.role: the computational objects the claim is about

method: analysis.py enumerates all 196 two-colour (blocks 1-3) and 1728 three-colour (blocks 1-2) neighbour-independent substitution rules, iterates each from a single cell of colour 1 until the word has 131072 symbols (or 60 steps), and counts distinct factors of length 1..14 with a sorted rolling-code method. It generates rule 30 from a single black cell with big-integer bit operations, taking the central 40001 cells of row 20000 and the first 65536 centre-column cells, and applies the same count. It also measures what share of the centre column's length-14 factors appear in any binary substitution word, and runs the one-cell-per-cell neighbour-dependent substitution systems for rules 90 and 30 against the direct CA for 1000 steps. Runtime about 19 s.

measured.unit: maximum number of distinct length-14 factors over all 1924 neighbour-independent substitution words (threshold 225)

caveats: The impossibility half is tested on the two complete enumerated families named in the book's own discussion (p. 83), not for arbitrarily long replacement blocks or alphabets; the complexity gap (at most 157 distinct length-14 factors versus 14922-16034 for rule 30) is a finite proxy for the theorem that fixed points of morphisms have polynomially bounded subword complexity.

The subword-complexity criterion treats any word with p(14) <= 225 as repetitive-or-nested; the words with the largest complexity (e.g. 0 -> 0, 1 -> 011, p(n) = 2,4,6,9,13,...,81) are non-primitive morphic words whose complexity grows faster than linearly but far below that of rule 30, consistent with the known n log n / n^2 classes for such words.

The neighbour-dependent half is near-definitional: a substitution system whose single output cell depends on the cell and its two neighbours is a cellular automaton; the test confirms it reproduces rules 90 and 30 exactly for 1000 steps, which is what the book's figure shows.

The length-14 factor share result (at most 0.5% of rule 30's centre-column factors occur in any binary substitution word) is reported as a direct check that none of the enumerated systems reproduces rule 30's sequence under the identity encoding; other encodings were not explored.
